extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques / readers of a 'Book of Proof' style textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, classify, and prove properties of relations (reflexive, symmetric, transitive); work with equivalence relations, equivalence classes, partitions, and the integers modulo n; determine well-definedness of operations on classes and construct/compare equivalence relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is reflexive if for every x ∈ A we have xRx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check reflexivity: verify xRx holds for all elements; if it fails, produce an element x ∈ A with (x,x) ∉ R. Examples: equality (=) and the divides relation (|) on integers are reflexive. Exercise prompts explicitly: 'Is R reflexive? If a property does not hold, say why.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on A is symmetric if xRy implies yRx for all x,y ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check symmetry: assume xRy and show yRx always follows; to disprove give x,y with xRy but not yRx. Examples: equality and 'same parity' are symmetric. Use counterexamples when a property does not hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on A is transitive if (xRy ∧ yRz) implies xRz for all x,y,z ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check transitivity: assume xRy and yRz and deduce xRz; to disprove provide x,y,z with xRy and yRz but not xRz. The textbook demonstrates truth-table-style reasoning in trivial cases and uses transitivity in proofs (e.g., proving [a] ⊆ [b]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence relations express a notion of 'sameness' (equality, same parity, congruence mod n, same degree of polynomials). To prove R is an equivalence relation, show the three properties hold. Exercises ask to prove various relations (e.g., ≡ (mod n), |x−y|<1 modified cases) are equivalence relations or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class [a] (definition and computation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation R on A, the equivalence class containing a is [a] = { x ∈ A : xRa }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute [a] by collecting all elements related to a (examples: [2] = {2,4} under 'same parity' on {−1,1,2,3,4}; classes for ≡ (mod n) are [0],[1],..., [n−1]). Use Theorem 11.1: [a] = [b] iff aRb, and use that when listing classes or showing equality of classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes form a partition (partition criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of equivalence classes { [a] : a ∈ A } is a partition of A: nonempty subsets whose union is A and whose pairwise intersections are empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove the equivalence classes form a partition, show (1) union over a ∈ A of [a] equals A (every x ∈ A lies in [x]), and (2) if [a] ≠ [b] then [a] ∩ [b] = ∅ (contrapositive proof using symmetry/transitivity). Conversely, any partition of A defines an equivalence relation by putting xRy iff x and y lie in the same block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of relations by combination of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations on a set can be catalogued by which of reflexive/symmetric/transitive properties they satisfy (there are 2^3 = 8 possible combinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples for each combination (e.g., equality, ≤, |, congruence mod n, etc.). The text encourages completing a table of examples for the missing combinations and notes some redundancies (e.g., ≤ and | may share the same pattern). When asked which properties hold, provide reasons or counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of equivalence relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If R and S are equivalence relations on A, then R ∩ S is also an equivalence relation on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: show reflexive, symmetric, and transitive properties are preserved under intersection (elementwise). The text gives the R2∩R3 = R4 example. Use this to produce new equivalence relations from known ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of equivalence relations (non-preservation warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The union R ∪ S of two equivalence relations need not be an equivalence relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask to prove or provide counterexamples. Do not assume closure under union; check each property if asked. Use small finite-set examples to exhibit failure of transitivity or other properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness of operations on equivalence classes (consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions that operate on representatives of classes (e.g., [a] + [b] = [a+b], [a]·[b] = [ab] in ℤ_n) must be independent of the choice of representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove well-definedness show that if [a] = [a'] and [b] = [b'] then [a+b] = [a'+b'] (similarly for products). The book demonstrates this for multiplication in ℤ_n using congruence arithmetic: a ≡ a' (mod n), b ≡ b' (mod n) ⇒ ab ≡ a'b' (mod n) so [ab] = [a'b']. Exercises include proving the analogous statement for addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing the smallest equivalence relation containing R (equivalence closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a reflexive and symmetric relation R on a finite set A, one can define S by declaring xSy when there exists a finite chain x R x1 R x2 ... R xn R y; S is the smallest equivalence relation containing R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise outlines the construction (path/connectivity closure), asks to prove S is an equivalence relation and that R ⊆ S, and to show minimality/uniqueness: any equivalence relation containing R must also contain S. Use this when asked to 'close' a relation under transitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting relation size from uniform equivalence class size
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is an equivalence relation on finite A and every equivalence class has cardinality m, then |R| can be expressed in terms of m and |A|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise asks to derive a formula for |R| (count ordered pairs in R) using the number of classes (|A|/m) and that each class contributes m^2 ordered pairs. Use partition/counting techniques to express |R|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation from A to B (generalized relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation from A to B is any subset R ⊆ A × B; we write xRy for (x,y) ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagramming guidance: draw labeled nodes for both A and B and arrows from elements of A to elements of B for which the pair is in R (example: membership relation ∈ as a relation from A to P(A)). This generalizes relations on a single set and is the setting for defining functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as a special relation (definition and criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is a relation f ⊆ A × B such that for each a ∈ A there is exactly one ordered pair (a,b) ∈ f. Domain = A, codomain = B, range = { f(a) : a ∈ A }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To verify a given subset of A×B is a function: check existence and uniqueness of the output for every input a ∈ A (vertical line test intuition). Examples: f(n)=|n|+2 as a relation from ℤ to ℕ. Use this definition when converting graphs/sets of pairs into function notation and when proving properties about functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof techniques and strategies used in this chapter
rubrics_metrics.description: Common proof methods: direct proof, contrapositive, element-chasing with set definitions, and use of prior properties (reflexive/symmetric/transitive) to deduce class equalities or partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Theorem 11.1 uses all three properties to show [a]=[b] iff aRb via subset arguments; Theorem 11.2 uses a contrapositive proof to show distinct classes are disjoint. Exercise advice implicitly given: when a property fails, provide explicit counterexamples; when showing closure/well-definedness, express representatives and use divisibility/congruence algebra as in ℤ_n arguments.
